subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I thank the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson) for relinquishing part of the time allotted to him so that I may have a few words to say before six o'clock. With what he has had to say I am to a large extent in agreement. Knowing that he comes from a family of distinguished and eminent lawyers, I think that we can probably take his remarks with respect to the legal profession with a little bit of salt. However, I agree with him as to members' salaries, and what member in this house does not agree with him? With respect to other things, of course, we should like to have co-operation.
We should like to limit speeches in this house to thirty minutes so that we may be permitted to leave this chamber by ten o'clock in the evening and not have to stay until eleven o'clock every night. If he will use the same forensic ability with his party on that matter we shall achieve that goal. I know the government is not desirous of throwing any weight behind this, because they are not anxious to put any pressure of their majority on the opposition. They want to give them every opportunity, but I am sure that if he will use his ability, which I envy, we shall accomplish that.
I should like to say a word on behalf of my constituency, which has probably the unique distinction of being the only constituency in Canada which is wholly south of the United States. A constituency is only about as good as the people that live in it. The people in our constituencies-and when I say "our constituencies" I mean the constituencies of Essex East, Essex South and Essex West- are showing their ability, their kindness, their large-heartedness at this present time. Because of our geographical situation we, like other constituencies bordering on the great lakes, are having considerable difficulty at the present time. As soon as the floods became manifest in our area an engineer was sent immediately to the area, by air, to make a survey. He has reported back. Subsequently the Minister of National Health and Welfare

(Mr. Martin), the hon. member for Essex South (Mr. Clark) and I have interested ourselves daily in that subject, and have attended meetings of the citizens group formed in the constituency of Essex East, and which is doing such a remarkable job.
I would say, in fact, that they are doing a heroic job, working day and night under great hardships to keep the flood waters back. They are not always successful, because there have been occasions when the flood waters have poured in over the dikes and over the waterfront of lake St. Clair, covering the main highway to a depth of about two feet. However the provincial government has seen its responsibility, and it, too, is doing a good job. There is an engineer in attendance to give advice, and he has been working closely with the local committee.
In my own constituency of Essex West, along the Detroit river I was instrumental in getting the towns of La Salle and Sandwich West to start an organization. The organization has been continuing and has done a good job in laying plans which would become effective in the event of an emergency. I am sure that if the provincial government finds that the problem becomes so great it cannot cope with it, it need only make application and it will be given every consideration by the House of Commons, as was done in connection with the Fraser valley and Winnipeg floods, and the fire at Rimouski.
Because of our geographical location we have things of great value. I am not particularly interested in discovering what is wrong with the area; my chief wish is to point out any error there may be and then to take every step possible to see that the error is corrected. I wish, further, to emphasize that which is good in the area-and there are many things. I thought this was best expressed by an hon. member of this House of Commons who visited the area, in company with fifty other members. On a bright Sunday morning they went down along the Detroit river to Amherstburg, and up through Harrow and Leamington. Passing through a sunny and rich farming area they saw mile upon mile of fruit trees in blossom, acres upon acres of hothouses in which cucumbers and tomatoes as well as other vegetables were being propagated under glass.
Upon his return to this city I asked him what he thought of what he had seen. With vigorous gesticulations he said, "No, no, no; what I saw I don't believe!" That, I think, best expresses the feelings of those who have seen the rich agricultural district in that area, as well as the great industrial plants.
The Budget-Mr. D. F. Brown Most of all however we pride ourselves on the friendliness of our people, a condition being commented upon each day. Only yesterday it was expressed to me in this building by a person of high rank who only recently in his official capacity had visited Windsor. He told me that of all the places in Canada he had visited, he found the people of that area the most hospitable and the most friendly that he had encountered anywhere.
I do not say that in a boastful fashion, but state it merely as a fact, because I believe to a large extent we have acquired some American traits of character, of which that is one.
I pointed out some time ago that in the area we have large industries, and I should like to refer to that fact for a moment. We have large automobile industries, large pharmaceutical plants and large chemical plants. Then, in association with the automobile industry there are sixty or seventy large and small feeder plants producing parts and equipment being fed to the automobile industry. Those industries have been operating in the area for many years. I believe it is safe to say that in that part of Canada there are more mechanical and chemical engineers per capita than in most other parts. They have acquired the knowhow of the industry. They are familiar with the technique. They are easily accessible to the United States which, either through our tunnel or across our suspension bridge, is only about five minutes away. In that length of time one can go from the heart of the city of Windsor to the heart of the city of Detroit, and he is at once accessible to the large technical ability of not only Detroit but the whole of the United States, because the automobile industry is concentrated in that American city.
Labour in the Windsor area is the same as in any other part of Canada. For the most part the workmen are hard-working, sincere and home-loving. They want nothing more than comfortable accommodation, enough to eat, and the hospitality and warmth of their homes. They have been trained not only in the universities of the area, but in those of the rest of Canada. They have had the advantage of one of the best technical schools in Canada, the W. D. Lowe school, formerly known as the Windsor-Walkerville technical school. This is a large educational establishment with competent instructors who are capable of training students for the automobile and other industries, including those connected with building trades in the area.
Then, we have available to us the University of Michigan located at Ann Arbor Wayne University and L'Assomption College So that labour is well trained; there is nt
1778	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. D. F. Brown reason why they cannot obtain the training they want to have. For the type of production on which Canadian prosperity and security is founded, there must be the utmost co-operation between labour and management. If we'are going to meet our production goals and maintain our present standard of living we must utilize all our productive resources. These cannot be used to the utmost in an atmosphere of suspicion and prejudice. We have had our difficulties in the past and we will probably have them in the future. It may be that because of our proximity to the United States our difficulties in my area are greater, but I think the rest of Canada can be most grateful that we have shown the ingenuity and stability to weather thest storms. I know that we will eventually come out on top.
If we are to overcome our difficulties there must be absolute co-operation. There must be a complete absence of fear, of suspicion and of prejudice. The Department of Labour has done a great deal in the way of providing machinery by which these things may be overcome, and I should like to speak on this for a few moments.
In February, 1943, the then minister of labour and the minister of munitions and supply set up an interdepartmental committee on labour-management committees. It is interesting to note that that good friend of labour, Mr. M. M. Maclean, a valued employee af the Department of Labour, was a member 3f that committee. The people of Canada Dwe a great deal to his efforts.
An advisory committee composed of representatives of trade union and employer groups was constituted to assist the interdepartmental committee. In March, 1943, the government jfficially decided to encourage and sponsor ;he formation of labour-management produc-;ion committees. Of course, that was for war purposes. It might be interesting to put on he record the principles underlying these :ommittees, and I quote from the report of he Department of Labour for the fiscal year inding March 31, 1944, page 44, as follows:
1.	The purpose of labour-management production ommittees should be to examine and consider neans to improve and increase production;
2.	The committee should be composed of repre-entatives from labour and management directly ngaged in production in the particular units or lants in which each committee functions. The umber of representatives of labour should be at ?ast equal to the number of representatives of lanagement. The representatives of labour should e chosen in a democratic manner, preferably from ae various departments or natural divisions of a nit or plant, rather than from the entire working Dree;
3.	The committee should be advisory and consul-itive. Management should examine carefully all ^commendations of labour representatives and, in ases where recommendations are not acceptable,


should provide adequate explanations. Similarly, the representatives of labour should examine carefully all recommendations of management and cooperate in making effective all recommendations endorsed by the committee and adopted by management;
4. The committees should concern themselves exclusively with problems of production, and should leave problems relating to wages, working conditions and similar matters, including grievances, to the appropriate collective bargaining procedure.
A labour-management co-operation service was established in May, 1947, as a section of the industrial relations branch of the Department of Labour to continue the work of the labour-management production committees. This committee was precisely what its name implies, a committee composed of representatives of labour and management to increase production and improve efficiency through greater co-operation between both groups. It is a joint enterprise. It is a two-way communication channel for the exchange of ideas and information on production problems. It is an agency making possible effective plant action on production, conservation, recreation, welfare, morale, absenteeism, safety, and a large number of other important problems. It in no way affects the right of a union to enter into bargaining agreements.
It is not a management plan for the promotion of company unions. It is not a labour plan for taking over the job of management. It is not a bargaining agency or a grievance committee. Wages, hours, working conditions and related matters are subjects for determination by collective bargaining procedures. If time permitted I could go on at some length to deal with the functions of this service.
I would certainly recommend this to industry which must take the lead in the city of Windsor in setting up as many labour-management production committees as is possible. The report issued this year indicates that 789 labour-management committees are operating in Canada affecting 306,427 workers. There is a total of 441 committees in the manufacturing section affecting a total of 164,154 workers. I am glad to be able to say that many labour-management committees are in operation in the automobile feeder plants in Windsor, but I am sorry to say that there does not seem to be the same co-operation in the plants of the big three which is necessary if we are to produce successfully for the betterment of Canada and create the utmost labour harmony.
I urge that industry take the lead in co-operation with the Department of Labour and see that such committees are set up at an early date. I should like to indicate what has been said by a worker in a plant, not in

the city of Windsor, about the work of these labour-management production committees, and I quote:
Things are done with a real team spirit around the place because we all know what's going on and why. Management tells us what's the trouble and we try to show them what's wrong. None of us are perfect. Any of us can be off the beam-but we can tell each other what's on our minds and there's no hard feelings. Sometimes we tell each other plenty. We make a better team when we all know the score.
Some companies throughout Canada in the operation of these labour-management production committees give certain incentives to the workers. I have in mind one company which in order to stimulate production started a competition between four teams of workers operating certain machines in the mills. The winners of this production competition were given a trip to interview the customers of that mill. They visited with the customers and saw what they wanted, and came back full of enthusiasm for the business in which they were engaged and in which they were partners. I think, too, these labour-management committees create confidence as between labour and management as nothing else can. When they get together they can do as we do in caucus, and explain matters frankly and honestly. I think if we are honest and sincere with each other-and this applies to management and labour-we will have greater industrial harmony.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while addressing my humble remarks to the house today, I do not so much propose to comment on the budget as such, as to submit certain statements on our immigration policy.
Nevertheless, after listening the the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) on April 24 last, I thought it might perhaps be appropriate to put a few suggestions to him.
In a speech which will go down in the history of his party, he indicated to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) how to economize something like $315 million. On page 1569 of Hansard, the member for Moose Jaw suggests that the members of the house should begin by setting an example and reducing the length of the sessions so as to have one session a year, without regard to existing conditions.
55704-113J
The Budget-Mr. Maltais
Since the hon. member has raised this matter without indicating the steps that should be taken to shorten the long sessions of parliament, I wonder why, in his campaign to curtail expenditures, the hon. member did not suggest that the redistribution committee, set up to inquire into the distribution of seats in the house allotted to each province, stick to the letter of the Canadian constitution. Since according to the constitution, the matter of distribution must again be examined in the light of the last census and since according to that same constitution my hon. friend's province is liable to lose five seats as a result of the same census, I would have thought that my hon. friend from Moose Jaw would have asked the house to stick to the constitutional formula and thus save approximately $300,000 in the next two parliaments.
As the hon. member for Moose Jaw stated, it is fitting that members of the house should themselves set the example in curtailing expenditures. I hope that he will be the first to practise what he preaches when the opportunity arises.
In the same speech, he urged the Minister of Finance to delete from the estimates item No. 42, where an amount of $500,000 was voted in order to help the maple syrup producers in the province of Quebec. This aid is granted by the government to help our producers replace the equipment used in the manufacturing of maple products and allow them to export their wares. This industry brings every year into Canada several million dollars, and I do hope that the government will continue to advise parliament to adopt a measure which is so beneficial to our farmers.
While studying the estimates of the same department, the hon. member might have come across the fact that not one among the Ontario or Quebec members tried to suggest that items 46 and 47 of these estimates should be reduced or suppressed altogether because they applied to the western provinces. As far as I am concerned, I have only the most superficial knowledge of the difficulties encountered by our fellow Canadians living in the prairies; I would be loath to see them deprived of the improvements which might be brought to them, thanks to the aid of the federal government. In return, I am sure the hon. member would not wish to adopt, towards my province, an attitude I would be reluctant to take towards any other province.
So much for that. I will not deal any further with the other suggestions made in that same speech since I feel no other mem-
1780	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Maltais ber in this house would want a reduction in the rates of family allowances, old age pensions or in any other social legislation.
Mr. Speaker, I consider the financial administration of the government to be highly important and I am one of those who have confidence and who believe that no country in the world has a better reputation than Canada, from a financial point of view.
The present government has, for a very large part, presided over the destinies of the nation since the dark days of the years 1931-1935 to the present period. During these 17 years that separate us from the "great darkness," Canada has taken an active part in a world war. We were victorious in that war and, if peace is not yet ours, at least we did not have to undergo the tragic crises which were the lot of the other nations with which we shared that victory.
This government, which longed then, like every other free nation, for an era of peace, was soon faced with the threat of new communist aggression and compelled to look, with the co-operation of friendly countries, for a new way of once again preserving world peace, which was threatened by an enemy more terrible than the one we had just defeated.
In seeking this new protection in alliances with other nations, it was imperative that we should assume certain obligations and new responsibilities which, during these last few years, have obliged the government to ask parliament for those appropriations as the price of our security.
Of course such expenses bear heavily upon the Canadian people. But we all hope that our collective effort will show any potential enemy that aggression would be a bad risk and that it would be preferable to settle our differences at a round table.
Many of us are asking ourselves just how far our defence preparations should go in view of the huge sums contained in the estimates. Such a question, Mr. Speaker, deserves an answer because the taxpayers want to know at times where their money goes. We would be on the wrong course if an arms race was our only aim. It is therefore important that the different countries coordinate their efforts so that each dollar spent for common defence be used where it is required and so that no country be called upon to contribute more than is necessary to pay this insurance premium for our common protection.
[Mr. Maltais.J

Canada.today is doing its heavy share and the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance inevitably reflects that fact. And in spite of this international situation which continually requires that ransoms be paid as protection against the forces of war, our government has passed social legislation which, in certain respects, goes further than any legislation existing elsewhere.
There again, tremendous amounts must be provided in order to maintain these social services, such as family allowances, unemployment insurance, pensions for the blind, old age pensions and our national health program. These are dangerous and fascinating times. Our prosperity, fashioned with hope and anxiety, has reached a peak we had never dreamed to attain during the present generation.
The various provincial governments each claim the glory of governing the most prosperous province. The future looks so bright that some of them become dazzled like the Duplessis government in Quebec, for instance, who are led to believe they have discovered the province of Quebec.
In all this atmosphere where prospects of a golden age join with uncertainty, where the forces of peace are locked in a constant struggle with the forces of war, the present government is able to bring down a balanced budget, to pay the cost of our defence and our national welfare and at the same time, which is quite surprising, to reduce our public debt. This wise government which has succeeded in stabilizing the cost of living, in spite of what our Progressive Conservative friends may say, has surprised them to such an extent that the surplus of the Minister of Finance is a riddle to them they are unable to explain.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the wise administration of our present government in this dangerous prosperity.
Let us consider the immigration problem. The speech made in this house on March 10 last by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) prompts me to do so. Needless to say, I do not share all the views he expressed on this occasion, nor am I able to find any reasons which might justify the request submitted by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce on page 13 of its last brief to the effect that many more immigrants be admitted into this country than we are now receiving.
I certainly do not hesitate to state with Philippe Roy of L'Action Catholique that, in our day, immigration is spoken of in the name of justice and human kindness, or of a more rational distribution of the world's population, and that as Christians we must support the principle of immigration.

I am therefore speaking of the manner in which that principle should be applied in our country, rather than of the principle of immigration itself.
At page 290 of Hansard, the hon. member for Spadina stated as follows:
Today a nation more than twice as large in population as it was in 1913, and many times as strong, is taking in only half the number of immigrants we took in at that time. I merely point out to the house that it is time we burst these bonds of caution. We have to take a firm stand in this country on immigration because we can produce more homes, more suits of clothing, more pairs of shoes and more loaves of bread.
And a little further down:
I am convinced that the country wants more of the right kind of immigration, the kind that we have been getting particularly this year.
Mr. Speaker, I respect the hon. member's opinion, but I believe that our immigration policy not only should be carefully selective, but it should also adapt itself to economic, social and political conditions in Canada.
Confronted with the huge geographical spaces of our country, people have often expressed various opinions concerning the best possible solution to the problem of Canadian population. The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), speaking in British Columbia, expressed the hope that our population will one day reach 125 million. I feel that this is a rather high figure and I am inclined to believe that this represents more people than Canada could support.
For, in spite of the vastness of our country, one should not fail to take into account the following facts: vast regions are unable to support a large population. All the northern districts, from Hudson bay to Georgian bay, the north side of lake Superior, Great Slave lake, and including the whole Arctic region, which represents two-thirds of the whole surface of Canada, can hardly, except here and there, support a population. According to the dominion bureau ef statistics, after the 1931 census, the arable land in this country comprises no more than 352 million acres-i.e. scarcely 27-5 per cent of its total area.
Of this total, 163 million acres are already settled. The rest of the area as yet not settled represents land where the farmer who will settle there will undergo a great many difficulties, because of the climate, the nature of the soil or the very limited production he will be able to obtain.
Naturally, the greater part of this farm land is located in the western provinces but even there agriculture seems confined to
The Budget-Mr. Maltais wheat growing and part of these lands are already marginal. The serious drop in Saskatchewan's population, during the last decade, seems to indicate that special crops in the prairies are unable to support a heavy population.
That is to say that Canada's population cannot be determined on the basis of land area alone. Other factors must be considered, such as the development of our natural resources, our productive capacity, our industrialization and our economic conditions. Therefore, in the preparation of a long-term immigration plan, it would be important to inquire into all these conditions.
If we look up statistics, we find that we have had waves of immigration which went up and down according to the times. The years before the war of 1914 were characterized by a heavy flow of immigrants. From 1916 to 1923 there was a large drop in the number of immigrants, but immigration was again on the increase from 1924 to 1931, when it was practically shut off up to 1945.
It is interesting to note that from 1901 to 1931 Canada received more than 5 million immigrants, but that, during the same period of time, nearly 3,500,000 people left the country. There is no doubt that a great number of these immigrants went back to their own country or that they simply passed through Canada before going to the United States. However these figures show that our immigration policy did not have the results that we hoped it would have. It is therefore important that our immigration policy be adapted to economic conditions in this country.
The present industrial expansion should not be overestimated. Although the development of our natural resources allows us to foresee a bright future we must always keep in mind that our Canadian economy is strongly influenced by international market conditions and conditions in other countries. Furthermore that development of our resources might be misleading if our role consists merely in extracting the raw materials and selling them to other countries without establishing manufacturing industries.
Even today, despite the activity resulting from our defence effort and our economic expansion, each year we go through a critical period of unemployment about which we certainly cannot feel unconcerned. And our

The Budget-Mr. Maltais great labour unions have requested that there be no immigration whatever during those periods of unemployment.
On the other hand, the housing problem is very serious in Canada and I take advantage of this opportunity to ask the government to amend the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act and the National Housing Act, 1944, in order to allow more people in the middle classes and from rural areas to avail themselves of the benefits of these acts. Conditions and restrictions imposed, in certain rural areas, under this act make it very difficult to operate, at least in the constituency of Charlevoix, which I have the honour to represent. A great many Canadian families are looking for houses. The manpower necessary for the construction of these houses is available since at the end of February of this year there were more than 13,000 unemployed in the building trades alone. In a report published recently by the Department of Trade and Commerce, no serious shortages of building materials were anticipated for this year.
I believe the time has come to extend the compass of the present National Housing Act in order to deal with the present housing shortage.
And this housing situation is closely related to our immigration policy since we have a right to ask where these immigrants are expected to find a house.
Briefly, Mr. Speaker, while I congratulate the government on their careful and judicious selection of immigrants, I am unable to share the views of the member for Spadina and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce who are calling for a greater number of immigrants.
I repeat once again, our immigration policy should not only aim at a proper selection of immigrants but it should be consistent with economic conditions in this country having regard to our absorptive capacity, to the yearly recurrent periods of unemployment and to the housing problems we face at the moment.
As immigration is also under provincial jurisdiction, I think it would be important to establish an advisory committee, consisting of the various provincial governments, of the representatives of labour unions, of employers and of the different universities, with a view to helping the department to work out an immigration policy consistent with this country's political, social and economic conditions.

In this way in order to increase the population of Canada we should be able to lead immigrants into this country towards adopting the ideals we all share, that is, a great, happy Canada respectful of the rights of all its sections, such as the two main races of this country have undertaken to build up when history placed them side by side to form the Canadian people.

speechtext:
The nature of the 1952 budget, as presented by our very able Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), is significant of our expanding economy and of our important place in national affairs. It underlines what must be apparent to all of us, namely, that Canada is one of the great nations of the free world, and that the entire world is looking to us for more and more of that stability which is necessary if free institutions and our way of life are to survive.
The opposition members have attacked the budget as imposing excessive taxation. I think we must be realistic, and if we remember our national prosperity and our domestic and international commitments, then I think we must conclude that the rate of taxation as imposed by this budget is quite in keeping with Canada's ability to pay. If we wish to continue our social security program, furnish sufficient money for the orderly administration of government, have sufficient funds to develop our natural resources, and still maintain our defence expenditures, then it seems to me we must be prepared to make some sacrifices during this important period of world affairs.
The Minister of Finance has indicated that there will be this year an estimated expenditure of $4,270 million. I should like briefly to review what these expenditures are as they were outlined by the Minister of Finance. We are spending on national defence slightly over $2 billion; on our social security program and other pensions, nearly $1 billion. Interest on the national debt and payment to provinces amount to $650 million, and the general administration and other activities of government amount to approximately $650 million. I should like briefly to review these expenditures. We are spending on national defence slightly over $2 billion. I believe that all hon. members agree that Canada must play her full part in the defence of freedom in the world today.

The Minister of Finance has very wisely pointed out that the scale of the defence budget is determined by policies approved by this parliament. It is true that the administration of the defence department is most important; but after all, what we members of parliament decide is in the best interests of Canada must underlie the expenditures of national defence.
I am sure that all hon. members support the part Canada is playing in the United Nations. The vast majority of the members in this house approve of what Canada is doing in support of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I for one am prepared to accept the advice of the statesmen and military experts of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization as to what is necessary in order to preserve our freedom. I cannot believe that in the C.C.F. party there are many international experts whose advice we can trust implicitly. Let us not make the mistake of too little too late. The financial critic of the official opposition made a statement in this house which is to be found on page 1481 of Hansard. He said:
We should not expect men in the services to be interested in expenses, Mr. Speaker. I think we would be naive to expect that. It is not their job, but the job of parliament.
I cannot agree with that statement. I think there is great responsibility on men in the services to see that our dollars are wisely spent. We can vote money in this house, but after we have given careful consideration to it, and are sure that it is in the national interest, then I think we have the right to expect the men in the services to do their part. There is a responsibility on the part of the deputy minister of national defence, the assistant deputy ministers and on all other officers of the armed forces. I remember that the financial critic told us of the time when he was in the army, and how careful he was to see that no public money was wasted. I would say that it is rather presumptuous on his part to suggest that he was the only man of that type to be found in the armed services. I am sure that there are many other men of that type who are anxious to see that money which we vote for national defence is wisely spent. I sincerely believe that is the case in the Department of National Defence in Canada.
We have had long discussions in this house on national defence; we have had a defence expenditures committee; we have made a
The Budget-Mr. Robertson close study of the estimates of the Department of National Defence. I suggest to you that every opportunity is given to members of the opposition party to show what money is not being wisely spent.
I should like to congratulate the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and his department on their good judgment in picking Cobourg, Ontario, my home town, as the site of the new central ordnance depot. There can be no doubt that the department showed excellent judgment in this decision, because Cobourg has many advantages which make it the logical place for the establishment of such a project. We have ample room for expansion of this depot, should it be necessary; we have excellent rail, water and road facilities; we have an adequate supply of labour; we have excellent recreational facilities. In fact, I think that we have everything which will make this central ordnance depot a real success.
I should like briefly to review our expenditures on social security which amount to nearly $1 billion. I am sure that these expenditures are approved by the vast majority of Canadians. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) wisely said the other night that we must consider very carefully the amount of money we spend on social security. We must be very sure that we shall never have to regress in the payment of social security. It is true that the C.C.F. party demand even greater and greater expenditures on social security.
The leader of the C.C.F. party, speaking in the house not long ago, assailed the government because we are not spending as large a percentage of our national income on social security as we did some four or five years ago. It seems ridiculous to me, when we are in the midst of a vast rearmament program costing over two billions of dollars, that the leader of the C.C.F. would expect us to spend as large a percentage on social security as we did before. I believe the social security program is the greatest single contribution the Liberal party has made to good government in this country. I am sure that as soon as the country can afford greater social security benefits the Liberal party will see that these are brought into being.
There can be little discussion of the third item in the budget, that of the payment of the interest on the national debt, and payments to the provinces. We would be failing to fulfil our obligations if we failed to make these payments.
Coming to the fourth division of the expenditures as outlined in the budget, we find that $650 million is being spent on the general administration of government. I

I have in my hand the estimates tor this fiscal year, and when we look at the different columns, we see that there has been a decrease in the various departments of government amounting to $62,787,593. Our country is an ever-growing country, and it requires an increasing amount of money in order to run the government of the country in an efficient way. The government can be congratulated upon the real economies it has put into effect in the last year. While members of the opposition are always asking for decreased taxation, they ask continuously for greater and greater expenditures. We see that the financial critic of the official opposition has this to say:
I would state without hesitation that we do have in this country, despite our glowing figures, those grandiose figures, uneasiness, and the feeling that we have been on the crest of a boom year after year, and there is the fear that one day the boom will end and the reckoning come.

How often have we heard that prophecy over the last few years? Here is what the hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. White) had to say, as it is set out at page 1503 of Hansard:
Now that we have lost the markets for our agricultural products and prices are decreasing, I am wondering where the government is going to get all the money it needs.
And quoting the leader of the Social Credit party, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), we find that he said this, as it is set out at page 1494 of Hansard:
Fear of overproduction is beginning to manifest itself not only in the farming industry but also in many fields, in spite of the world's need for food, and other necessities of life, and in spite of hunger and suffering in many lands.
He goes on to say, as reported on page 1495:
Today farm prices, it is true, are relatively more fair in relation to taxes and interest rates; but the general price level is so high that there is widespread fear that the present abundant situation will come to a sudden collapse.
Just what advice should the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) take from the members of the opposition? Some are predicting a huge surplus while others are saying that our national production is falling away. If these latter people are right, then under our present taxation we will be budgeting for a deficit and even the financial critic of the official opposition says that that is not a good thing.
Our Minister of Finance has a wonderful and proud record to present to this house in the matter of debt reduction. Since 1947 he has reduced the national debt by $2,344 million, with an interest saving to the taxpayers of Canada of $62 million. I ask hon. members of the opposition what good businessman, under similar circumstances, would not do exactly as the Minister of Finance has done. Is it not true that the generally accepted business principle is to pay your debts during periods of prosperity? I have never heard anyone speak to the contrary.
The position taken by others is that we should have a planned debt reduction. What does that mean? It means that if the advice of those members of the opposition who are crying hard times is taken we will have to tax the people of Canada even more. Why is it not reasonable to adopt a pay-as-you-go budget and plan for a balanced budget? If our prosperity exceeds our expectations then I submit that that is the time to make payments on our national debt. Why should we saddle posterity with the debts of our generation?
I have noticed that the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) is becoming the official spokesman for the Conservative party
The Budget-Mr. Robertson at political meetings throughout the country. I congratulate the hon. member upon his rapid promotion within the party, but after reading some of his speeches I feel that I cannot congratulate the Conservative party upon their selection.

He was asked this question by Mr. Baldwin:
I believe the Progressive Conservative party voted with the C.C.F. for price control. Can you tell me why?
The answer of the hon. member was as follows:
We did-
And then he continues:
We supported the C.C.F. amendment because we wanted to register protest against the "do-nothing" policy of this government, and this was the only vehicle open to us. We might say that we were not subscribing to any particular form of control, and certainly not the old control.
Their advice-flexible controls selectively applied. That is the way the Conservative party would have handled the inflationary

We have heard many
members of the Conservative party speaking in the house and attacking the government for removing the name "dominion" from certain statutes of Canada. They almost suggested that they were the only people who were proud of their British ancestry and of British traditions. Let me tell them that there are many members of all parties who are proud of that heritage. When we review the situation we find that not long ago their great party was known as the dominion Conservative party, but today we find that they are glad to call themselves the national Conservative party. Could we have a better example of double talk than that?	'

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When was it called dominion?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You must have known because you had something to do with changing the name of your party. The members of the Conservative party are always preaching economy, and then they ask for larger and larger expenditures. I have already outlined some of the demands on the government which they have made. The Minister of Finance pointed out in his review that had the people of Canada accepted them in the last election our taxes would have been $1 billion more than they are under a Liberal government.
Finally they suggest to the people of Canada that we could have our national security program, that we could have ample money for national defence, that we could have all the money necessary for the orderly discharge of the business of this country and still offer the people of Canada a substantial reduction in the rate of taxation. Can you imagine a greater fraud being perpetrated on the Canadian people than the present policy of the Conservative party? I should like to tell you, Mr. Speaker, what other people think of the government of Canada and its accomplishments. I quote the Monetary Times of March, 1952, commenting on the return to parity of the Canadian dollar:
Nearly everybody's happy that the Canadian dollar is back to parity with its American cousin.


It's more than a matter of national pride. A par dollar will help reduce the cost of what we Canadians import from the United States. In this way parity is a contribution to a reduction in the cost of living in this country.
And the London Times under date of April 15, speaking of Canada's position, says:
Clearly Canada is exceptionally favoured by fortune: but prosperity as well as adversity is a test of statesmanship, and much credit is due to Mr. St. Laurent's government for the happy condition of the nation's affairs. Canada may be congratulated the more wholeheartedly by her friends because her financial strength helps to buttress the entire free world.
Those of us who were privileged last evening to hear our distinguished visitors from the United States, Senator Gillette and Mr. Justice Roberts, will remember the tribute they paid to the economy of our country. I for one prefer to accept their opinion and that of such newspapers as I have quoted rather than the opinion of the official opposition or any other party in this house.
The financial critic of the official opposition accused the government of debauching our currency. He reminds me of the juryman who was unable to agree with the other eleven jurors. In exasperation he said, "I have never seen eleven such stubborn men." I submit that the financial critic of the opposition is in exactly the same category and that everyone is not out of step but the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). I do not wish to suggest for one moment that we have no problems in this country. We have had many problems; we are facing grave problems today and we will have great problems in the future. But I do suggest that the government has met those problems of the past effectively and, may I add, courageously.
We have certain problems in my own county of Northumberland which are causing some concern today, and I should like to mention them briefly. One is the fact that in Cobourg and the next largest town in the county, Campbellford, we have some unemployment. We know the development of the ordnance project at Cobourg will do much to relieve the unemployment situation in that town. In Campbellford the main difficulty is unemployment in the textile industry, which is general throughout the world. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) very ably pointed out that the depression in the textile industry was world-wide, but I was happy to note that he predicted some improvement in the near future. I am sure the government will give every consideration to the needs of the textile industry and will do what can be done to help it.
We have noted some decline in agricultural prices. That is causing some concern in my

riding, which is partly rural. The reasons for this decline are many and varied. Some are seasonal; some arise from overproduction and some from the loss of the British market. Some result from the foot-and-mouth disease, and some are a combination of all these. No one could expect the top prices we have been receiving for agricultural products to continue indefinitely, but I would like to impress upon this house my belief that it is most important that we see the returns from farm products do not fall below a reasonable level. I am convinced that we cannot enjoy real prosperity in this country unless our agriculturists are enjoying a decent scale of living. I endorse the farm price support policy of the government, which I believe is doing much to stabilize conditions in the country today.
The chief worry in connection with agriculture at the present time has to do with the dairy industry, and I want to speak particularly of the cheese situation. I listened with great interest a few evenings ago to the very interesting speech on cheese by the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart). We have long recognized him as one of the leading authorities in this house on the fishing industry and I am pleased to see that he is so versatile. I could not agree with everything the hon. member said regarding cheese, but I do believe it is not the sole responsibility of the federal government to look after the cheese situation in Canada today. The difficulty developing in connection with cheese is a cause of great concern to all connected with the dairy industry, but we know that the Ontario cheese marketing board has asked the government of Ontario for authority to look after the marketing of cheese in this country. It is regrettable that at the present time there is a very poor market; but I am sure if the provincial government, after considering the situation that is developing, would come to the federal government and say, "The condition is serious. Can we not work out some co-operative effort to aid the cheese men," this government as usual would lend a sympathetic ear to such an appeal.
I would like to see a greater advertising campaign undertaken by the makers of Ontario cheese, in an effort to sell more cheese in Canada. I think we have the finest cheese produced anywhere in the world, but it is rather disheartening to learn that Canadians eat less cheese per capita than almost any other people in the world. If the Ontario cheese marketing board would undertake an extensive selling campaign I believe that could do much to relieve that situation. I do bespeak on behalf of the cheese makers of
The Budget-Mr. Robertson Ontario every consideration and assistance on the part of the government, should that assistance become necessary.
There is another matter I would like to discuss at this time. The hon. member for Kent, Ont. (Mr. Huffman) made a plea in this house not long ago for the rural mail carriers of Canada, and I would like to support that plea wholeheartedly. I feel that this government might well set up a special committee to study this problem. Under our present system, in order to obtain a contract it is necessary to put in a tender at such a low rate that there is actually no profit for the contractor. In effect these men must cut each other's throats. I do not think that is a good method by which to award rural mail contracts. Surely some alternative could be worked out to give a new deal to these people. The cost of automobiles has greatly increased. In the spring and winter months the roads are often in bad condition, and it is impossible for the rural mail carriers to maintain their vehicles in good condition at the present rates. I would respectfully suggest to the government that this committee be set up as soon as possible to see if some alternative satisfactory method of awarding contracts cannot be worked out.
There is one other matter which I should like to bring to the attention of this house, and it concerns the Canadian Farm Loan Board. In my opinion the present policy of this board is most inadequate to meet present needs. I know of numerous instances in my county where farmers with valuable farms have been unable to raise $3,000 or $4,000 mortgages. We know that the government is lending up to 90 per cent on urban dwellings. Why should we discriminate against the farmer, which in effect is what we are doing if we do not change the Canadian Farm Loan Board regulations as they exist today. I do not believe that those regulations have been revised for many years, and we all know of the difference in value which exists now as compared with the time when these regulations were put into effect.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that when I spoke in this budget debate a year ago I said that the future of Canada was bright, and that the affairs of this country were in good hands. Everything which has happened since that time only serves to make that conviction stronger. In fact, we must admit that our vision could not perceive of the great developments and expansion that was to take place in Canada. I believe that if the Canadian people prepare to work hard and to work together they can produce in Canada an unsurpassed heritage. I am convinced that our government has played a notable part in the progress which

The Budget-Mr. Drew Canada has made. I believe that the government merits the confidence it enjoys amongst the majority of the people of this country. From my experience and my association in this house I am prepared to say that the actions of the government are motivated by one simple desire, to do, at all times, what is in the best interests of Canadians and in the best interests of Canada.

I propose to deal with this because it is not the first time that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has placed on the record similarly inaccurate statements in the same way. If I do not deal with them, particularly in view of the repetition of those statements tonight, I know that the minister will follow his usual practice of saying that his statements were not challenged, and therefore it must be assumed that they were accurate. He will, of course, disregard the fact that he spoke until eleven o'clock, and that no opportunity was afforded to deal with it. The minister had special reasons for knowing how completely inaccurate his statements were, but it is not only the inaccuracy of his statements in which I am interested; I am equally interested in the very obvious reasons for the introduction once again at this time of something which had no conceivable bearing of any kind on the motion which was before the house last Monday.
The motion under discussion at that time proposed that consideration be given to the adjustment of family allowances to bring them in line with the greatly increased cost of living in this country. Whether that


would be wise or unwise is obviously debatable. One member of the C.C.F. party attracted considerable attention only a few days ago when he argued that there should be a reduction in the over-all payment of family allowances. The minister responsible thinks that there should be no change. Others consider that if the figure originally chosen was correct, then adjustments should be made so that the family allowance will represent the same amount in real buying power. It should not be open to question in this house that each of those three points of view could be sincerely held, without any question being raised about the belief in the principle that family allowances should be paid. Nevertheless, although I did not introduce the motion, nor in fact had the resolution on this occasion been introduced by a member of the Conservative party, the Minister of National Health and Welfare took the opportunity to once more attempt to create the false impression that I was opposed to the payment of family allowances. In support of this contention he read from a newspaper report covering part of something I had said nearly eight years ago.
One might well wonder why this persistence. One might well wonder why the return to something that took place during the war years. One might well wonder why the minister returned to something that took place before we finally met here in a dominion-provincial conference in August, 1945, in response to the request of the government of Ontario, conveyed to the government of Canada by myself as premier of that province at that time. Even if the minister had correctly interpreted my position at that time, it would have had no bearing whatever upon the motion before the house.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It sure is.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Speaking on behalf of the Ontario government, and before any of the discussion took place which the minister now seeks to interpret so inaccurately once again, I made it clear over and over again that we believed in the principle of family allowances and that we wished to discuss the subject with the dominion government. As the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) well knows, in writing and otherwise we proposed to the then prime minister of Canada that there should be conferences to deal with the broad problems of social security. Those who remember what took place know that the letter which I wrote to the Prime Minister of Canada was used by him as the basis for the discussions. He sent that letter to the premiers of the other provinces, with the suggestion that this be taken as the basis of our subsequent meetings.
At that time the war seemed to be drawing to a close and the Ontario government-and for that matter most of the other provincial governments-were expressing their concern at that time about the danger to our constitutional position if centralization of taxation and control continued to follow the pattern which had developed during the war. During the war we had all agreed to the suspension of many constitutional prerogatives of the provincial governments to facilitate the war effort. We were doing our utmost, however, to persuade the dominion government to hold conferences before the end of the war so that after the war was over our democratic federation should return to its historic position of checks and balances between the dominion and provincial governments, as laid down in the British North America Act. I objected-and I was not alone in that objection-to the action of the dominion government in dealing with this subject of family allowances without consulting the provinces and in dealing with that subject as though the payment of family allowances were merely a matter of dollars and cents and not a social problem of the utmost importance to all our people.
The Budget-Mr. Drew
As has been the case over and over again when we have sought to emphasize the constitutional position, the government employed all its propaganda power, used at the expense of the people, to convey the impression that we were impeding their course which, one would almost think, to hear their statements, had by that time gathered something of the atmosphere of divinity.
In the very speech to which the Minister of National Health and Welfare referred last Monday, I said as long ago as August 9, 1944:
We are in favour of every proper step being taken to encourage large and healthy families. We believe in sound provisions for family allowances and social security.
That was nearly eight years ago. Surely those words are definite enough. But they were studiously disregarded by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, as they have been over and over again when he seeks to give the very opposite impression to this house-and, of course, outside of it with even wider disregard for the accuracy of his statements. As he well knows, that has been my position, as it was the position of the Ontario government, at all times when this subject was under discussion. Nor is there any necessity for defining my position by any isolated statement of that kind. In public statements, in letters to the Prime Minister of Canada at that time, in personal discussions with him and in statements to the Ontario legislature, this subject was discussed many times. The Minister of National Health and Welfare is well aware of that fact.
Just to place on record exactly what our position was-and a position that I might say was well known to the dominion government at that time and since-I propose to quote from the record of what I said in the Ontario legislature on February 22, 1945, more than seven years ago and long before I was in this House of Commons. I shall continue to quote until I indicate that the quotation is ended because, of necessity, it is a fairly extensive quotation.
This government has from the beginning been convinced that family allowances are an integrated part of the whole question of social security, and has so stated. The members of this legislature will recall that I made this clear and definite statement on behalf of the Ontario government on August 9 last:
"We are in favour of every proper step being taken to encourage large and healthy families. We believe in sound provisions for family allowances and social security."
That was our position then. That is our position today. I have stated over and over again that we regard family allowances as one of the most important social services: that it is therefore within the exclusive constitutional jurisdiction of the provinces; that the provinces must be consulted if there is to be any effective administration of family

The Budget-Mr. Drew
allowances; and I have publicly urged over and over again that there be a dominion-provincial conference to settle the basis upon which the dominion and provincial governments of this country can best combine their legislative authority for the benefit of all our people.
The problem with which this and every other provincial government is faced has been stated most clearly by the Hon. Stuart Garson, Premier of Manitoba. I will quote his own words on the subject;
"We are still puzzled as to one of the most important points. . . We have no information before us which indicates conclusively whether the dominion government itself regards and justifies family allowances primarily as a social security measure, or as an instrument of federal fiscal policy . . .
It seems to me that the point here is that the dominion government in introducing family allowances without consulting the provinces, whose jurisdiction over the field of social services heretofore in practice has been considered almost exclusive, surely could not have intended to justify them solely or even primarily as a social service measure. As such they would constitute a federal intrusion in a provincial field of jurisdiction."
I would remind hon. members of this house that I have been quoting from the words of Hon. Stuart Garson, who at that time was premier of the province of Manitoba. I will now continue to quote from the record of the debate in the Ontario legislature:
I do not believe the situation could be more clearly stated. If family allowances are to be regarded solely or even primarily as a social service measure, then again to quote Mr. Garson's words, "They would constitute a federal intrusion in a provincial field of jurisdiction."
Now we are told by the minister responsible for the administration of this act that it is part of a broad system of social security. If that is so, and we have never been in any doubt that it was so, then this act is an intrusion upon the provincial field of jurisdiction without any consultation with the provinces. In fact the situation goes very much farther than that. Having disregarded the constitutional position of the provinces and their jurisdiction over social services in the introduction of the act, the dominion government has refused repeated requests from myself and other provincial premiers for a dominion-provincial conference to discuss this and other invasions of our authority.
I wish to assure the members of this legislature that we have at all times made it abundantly clear that we were not seeking to raise constitutional issues but that we were seeking to avoid constitutional difficulties in the future. I have made it clear, and I believe the premiers of other provinces have made it equally clear, that our purpose in insisting upon a dominion-provincial conference immediately is not to raise barriers against measures which will be for the benefit of our people but rather to make sure that we combine the full constitutional power of the dominion and provincial governments, so that whatever is done may not be upset subsequently by any one who wishes to test the validity of legislation of this nature in the courts. We also wish to make sure that the highly trained and competent social service workers in the different provinces have their part in the administration of any plans of social security which may be adopted.
Anyone with the least knowledge of family and child welfare knows that the health, housing, nurture and all the interests of human beings, hang

together in a well-integrated whole. You cannot deal with the human needs of a family today without relating closely all the resources in your social catalogue-maternal	care, nutrition, housing,
mothers' allowances, all forms of assistance, etc. So, your whole welfare security program cannot be done on a bits and pieces basis. It has to be unified and its administration rests with the provinces unless the whole basis of confederation is to be destroyed. . . .
That is the end of the quotation from the records of the debate in 1945.

No sooner had 1 made that statement than misrepresentations were repeated such as those which have been repeated here tonight, and were repeated on Monday night in regard to our position in relation to family allowances. For that reason I referred to this subject again only four days later in the Ontario legislature, on February 26, 1945, and to those who have apparently come into the house since I started to speak, that was over seven years ago. Again I quote from the record of what I said on that occasion, and again until I have indicated that the quotation is ended I shall be quoting from the record of the discussion in the Ontario legislature:
The statement I gave to the legislature last Thursday was not intended as a complete statement on this subject, nor was there any suggestion that it was intended to take the place of the remarks I proposed to make in the debate on the speech from the throne.
I did recall, however, our positive and very definite statement that "we are in favour of every proper step being taken to encourage large and healthy families. We believe in sound provisions for family allowances and social security."
In spite of our position having been stated so clearly, statements are still made that we are opposed to family allowances.
I referred to the iniquitous principle involved in the measure which has been adopted by the dominion government. My speech quite clearly was not referring to any opposition to family allowances. It was referring to the principle that family allowances are not part of social security and that they should be regarded as a mere economic question. We also believe it is an iniquitous principle that very large sums of money should be taken from the taxpayers of this or any other province to be paid for something which falls within the jurisdiction of the provincial governments, without consulting those provincial governments and establishing a proper basis of taxation and payment right across Canada.
At the time I said that we would oppose the course being followed by the dominion government, we had the unqualified assurance of the Prime Minister of Canada that there was going to be a dominion-provincial conference to discuss matters of this kind, and it was our intention to do everything within our power at that conference to assure that we have a proper system of family allowances and that the rights of the people of Ontario be protected.

Now may I come to the suggestion that we intend to take legal steps to prevent the dominion act going into effect. That is not our intention and it never has been our intention. I have said in this legislature and elsewhere many times that I do not believe that the dominion and provincial governments should get involved in legal technicalities, but rather that they should meet around the council table to work out their problems and find the very best solution in every case, so that their combined powers may find full expression for the advantage of the people of this country.
Our purpose is to have in this province the very best system of family allowances which can be worked out on the basis of the accumulated experience of every other jurisdiction which has already adopted this measure. As I said last week, we wish to join hands to combine our legislative power with that of the dominion government to assure the best social services which can be devised.
You will find that in a speech as recently as Saturday night, Mr. Claxton made it quite clear that this province has been co-operating in all the preliminary details necessary for carrying out such a measure under such terms as might be agreed upon. We have, in fact, set up the most modern methods of recording vital statistics, and have installed photographic devices which provide the government at Ottawa with every detail of our vital statistics for the very purpose of carrying out this or any other measure.
I believe it is an iniquitous principle that payments should be a mere baby bonus based upon the fact that a baby has been born. I believe that our people want real family allowances, in the accepted meaning of that term, for the maintenance, care training and upbringing of children, in a way that will assure the welfare of the children themselves. That is not accomplished by the present dominion act. We have the clear words of the Prime Minister of Canada, "The act does not in any way attempt to legislate in respect of family life." If it has nothing to do with family life, then how can it possibly assure the welfare of the children in those families which receive the money?
As you know, we have continued to press for a dominion-provincial conference right up to the opening of this session for the very purpose of bringing together the combined authorities of our governments so that in this, and every other case, no constitutional difficulties might arise and that everything should be done with full knowledge of the facts and with the certainty that what is undertaken will be carried out in the best interests of our people.
That is the end of the quotation which was taken from what was said in the Ontario legislature on February 26, 1945. I would point out that what the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) read had nothing to do with the question of whether or not we were in favour of family allowances. He was quoting from a speech which he now has in his hand'-and I welcome the fact that this has been brought out in the open, here, instead of simply knowing that it is being repeated with trimmings, as it has been repeated, with very unreliable trimmings over and over again in the past.
And may I say this, in so far as this is concerned, that I believe the Minister of National Health and Welfare knows his
The Budget-Mr. Drew Shakespeare well enough to recall that it was only when Iago was not exposed that he was really dangerous.
But, in so far as this is concerned, I do wish to go on with another aspect of the subject. The Minister of National Health and Welfare himself is either dealing with the question of family allowances or he is dealing with something else. And if he wants to raise other subjects, then let him be quite assured that, on that level, he will be inviting a course that would of necessity result in dealing with matters which have no relation to the subject which he pretends to be dealing with, and which he regards as of so much importance.
Those were not the only occasions upon which I spoke about this subject. It was discussed frequently. What is more, the subject was discussed with representatives of the dominion government. And they themselves came to realize that it would have been an iniquitous thing to have carried out their original plan, and simply appropriate money and hand out payments without any regard to the possibility that those payments might never be used for the benefit of the children. Therefore they came to the Ontario government, as they went to other governments, and they sought the assistance of their social service organizations to do the very thing that we had said should be done.
And it may be a matter of interest to know that the present Minister of National Health and Welfare has on different occasions commended the Ontario government for the manner in which it has carried out those services in co-operation with the dominion government. And the very minister who now repeats this statement that we were opposed to family allowances knows very well that it was under my direction, as premier of Ontario, that the instructions were given that those services should be made available.
It may very well be asked why the Minister of National Health and Welfare would raise this subject at this time. The purpose was clear. It was the same purpose which has prompted a number of members on the other side of the house for some years to do the same thing, and prompted another member here in this house tonight. Because those statements seemed so unworthy of notice, and were so palpably absurd, I must confess that I have not dealt with them as vigorously as I should. It seemed to me that, in themselves, they constituted the most severe criticism of those members who made them.

The Budget-Mr. Drew On looking back over the numerous occasions on which this utterly unfounded allegation has been made I find, however, that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has taken occasion to mention that I did not deal with his statement and that, therefore,
I must be regarded as accepting its accuracy. He knew perfectly well what the position was; but because of that attitude, because of the obvious reason for introducing a subject which had no relation to the motion before the house last Monday, I place these facts on the record today in a way that I have not attempted to do before, or have never thought that it was necessary to do since I entered this house.
I am well aware of the nature of the attacks which have been made upon me personally in regard to family allowances. Please do not think that these attacks, which are made from house to house, do not come back and are not accurately reported. Please do not think for one moment that I am not well aware of exactly the nature of the things that are being said in the different provinces, and which are being said in different provinces in entirely different ways.

We had an example yesterday afternoon in a speech made in this house when we heard the old catalogue of attacks upon different leaders of the Conservative party. There is not a member in this house who does not know of the shameful and shameless things that were said about one of the most brilliant Canadians who ever entered public life, the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen. I remember the things that were said about Sir Robert Borden, about Lord Bennett, about Mr. Manion, Mr. Hanson and Mr. Bracken. The time has come, yes the time is long overdue to place squarely where it belongs the full responsibility for this effort by officials and others of the Liberal party to undermine confidence in their political opponents by fair means or foul.
The quotations from what I said in the Ontario legislature, which I have already read, dealt with attacks of one kind which have been made here in this house and were made in this house more than seven years ago and also in the Ontario legislature. But I also found it necessary to deal with that other kind of attack, the charge that we were so closely associated with Quebec to the detriment of the rest of Canada. There is no hon. member who is frank who will not admit that he has heard that statement made here in this house and elsewhere. So that I may indicate what my position has been all the way through these discussions, I shall quote from the Hansard record of the debates of the Ontario legislature of April 15,	1948, as
follows:
The co-operation between the governments of Quebec and Ontario has covered a very wide field. We have been able to make satisfactory agreements, not only for the construction of new power plants on the Ottawa river, but also for additional supplies of electric power over and above existing contracts. We have established a wide measure of uniformity in different fields of taxation, and there has been the closest co-operation between such related departments of government as mining, lands and forests, highways and so on.
The governments of Quebec and Ontario have at all times, since the meeting of the dominion-provincial conference, in August, 1945, held similar views in regard to the importance of respecting the constitution which made this country a nation in 1867. On no single occasion, either at the first

The Budget-Mr. Drew meeting of that conference or at the meetings which followed, did either the government of Quebec or the government of Ontario express any opinion or put forward any proposal which did not recognize the desirability of general agreement to provide those services which will elevate the living standards of all the people of Canada wherever they may live.
It is only necessary to examine the statements made in different provincial legislatures this year to realize how disillusioned are some of those governments which submitted to the terms put forward by the dominion government without consulting the provinces. The governments which a year ago hailed the purchase price of their taxing rights as the dawn of new financial security for the provinces, are, in a number of cases, now forced to resort to new forms of taxation to meet their current financial requirements.
I believe the time is not far distant when those provinces which did give up their most important taxing rights for a fixed payment, without any compensating advantage, will come to the decision that the refusal of the governments of Quebec and Ontario to submit to such terms actually saved our federal system, without which there can be no sound basis for national unity in Canada.
I repeat exactly what I said then: The time will come when the people of this country will understand that it is extremely important for all Canadians that the British North America Act at least have the continuing existence which was assured by the fact that two of the provinces representing well over 60 per cent of the population of Canada did not abandon that division of authority which was so well created in 1867. Then I went on to refer to this attempt that had been made at that time in the Ontario legislature to criticize me for being too friendly with Quebec, for being too closely associated with them in what we were doing at that time. I quote again from the Hansard record of that day:
I regret any attempt should be made to criticize that co-operation. Before confederation these two provinces were one. Our history follows a parallel course through many long years. One of the most important questions before all of us today in Canada is whether we will fan the embers of past misunderstandings, or seek in every way we can to find a broader basis for co-operation and friendship with the common purpose of building a stronger and more united Canada, within which every province and everyone in them will share the many advantages and opportunities which Providence has placed at the disposal of this great nation.
What I have quoted shows the position I took, first of all in regard to family allowances, and second in regard to this allegation repeated over and over again that the government of Ontario was aligning itself too closely with Quebec, that they were becoming too intimate. Yes; on that very day it was said, as an attack, that I walked arm in arm with the premier of the province of Quebec.

My very first official call as premier of Ontario was on Premier Godbout of Quebec, to discuss the mutual interests of our two provinces. I have said publicly in the Ontario legislature and I repeat now, that unlike some of those who belong to the same party in other fields I found Premier Godbout most anxious to co-operate with the province of Ontario and ready to join hands in any way he thought he could at that time, in the interests of the two provinces.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is not one of us who on some occasion has not used words which taken from their context could convey a meaning entirely different from that which was intended. I will go further. There is not one of us, including the Prime Minister and the members of the government, who on some occasion has not used words that at a later date and in view of later events he would have chosen otherwise.

Is it more important to try to create good will and understanding in Canada or good will and understanding among distant countries in whom we are interested but whose welfare is not our concern as much as that of the country in which we live and which we are pledged to serve? I would remind you, Mr. Speaker, that not very long ago we listened to a Liberal member repeating these very statements, using such terms as "fraud" and "double talk" and words of that kind.
