Hear, hear.

And of course it should be applauded because it followed their pattern, and I would be surprised if it were not. But it is also interesting to note how unwelcome to the members who applaud in that way is any statement which deals with the conduct of which they have been guilty for so many years.
I have placed these matters on record, Mr. Speaker, and I go further and say this. There is not one member of this house who would not wish that at some time he might have put words in a different form.
Oh, oh.

That applies to the Prime Minister, to every member of the government, and I am sure to every Liberal member in this house. May I say this? No matter what words are used the question before the members in this house today is whether or not we are going to seek a basis of unity or try to destroy unity by picking out anything that will sow the seeds of discontent in this country of ours.
Mr. Speaker, is it not an interesting thing that we should be applauding the fact that two nations, which only a few short years ago were engaged with us in bitter conflict, are now free of the shackles imposed upon them after the war and that we are seeking
The Budget-Mr. Drew to lay the foundations of friendship with those nations at this time? True, we remember the conflicts that took place, but today we are seeking to build for the future by extending the hand of friendship to Germany and Japan, and other nations, in a common fellowship of nations for our own good. If it is logical, if it is sensible, that we should seek grounds of understanding in the international field, then surely it is unworthy of any Canadians who profess a belief in that course and at the same time follow a different course here in our own country. Certainly, there have been misunderstandings; certainly, there have been differences of opinion and violent differences of opinion; but it is the genius of our form of democracy and of our people that we are able to compose our differences and join hands in friendship in building for the better days ahead.
I ask hon. members to recall this fact. They are going back nearly eight years, as they have gone back for other periods of time and yet is it not significant that here in this building, on August 6, 1945, the representatives of the nine provinces which then made up Canada met to discuss the future of Canada with the representatives of the dominion government? Is it not significant that there were those that thought that the unity of purpose and common understanding between the representatives of Quebec and Ontario were too close for their satisfaction? Whether the allegation was right or wrong, that it was too close for their satisfaction, at least there was no doubt that there was real understanding between the governments of Ontario and Quebec in regard to the constitution and what it meant in protecting the rights of our people. May I go further and say that there was not a single provincial premier who disagreed with the position that we took at that time in regard to the importance of the constitution as a basis for national unity. One by one some of the provinces found it necessary to make financial arrangements, but that did not change their expressed belief that we should preserve the constitution intact in every way.
Now, with that background, with the fact that the representatives of Quebec chosen by democratic process within that province, met and found common ground-yes, and, according to those who sought to criticize us, close friendship-with representatives chosen by democratic process in Ontario, surely that is evidence of the way in which the affairs of this country can be operated in the best interests of the people of Canada. Those who talk so piously of national unity, and at the same time sow the seeds of suspicion and

The Budget-Mr. Drew distrust, not in relation to any subject under discussion but for another purpose clearly disclosed, those people are guilty of nothing less than a form of national sabotage. I repeat the words that I have used before:
One of the most important questions before all of us today in Canada is whether we wilt fan the embers of past misunderstandings, or seek in every way we can to find a broader basis for co-operation and friendship, with a common purpose of building a stronger and more united Canada, within which every province, and everyone in them, will share the many advantages and opportunities which Providence has placed at the disposal of this great nation.
We have great and important subjects to discuss, Mr. Speaker, and we can discuss them upon a factual and reasonable basis. There are two courses open. If members of the government depart from any subject before this house seeking to introduce other subjects for purposes so clearly unrelated to the matters in debate, then their real interest in national unity will be clearly expressed. The choice is theirs. There is no doubt about the fact that they have used anything that they thought would be of advantage, and no harm will be done in exposing openly anything that they have used secretly, and used over and over again. But the fact still remains that if we here in this country are sincere in our expression of belief in good will, in better understanding and friendship between peoples in distant lands, then the test of that sincerity will lie in the course that we follow right here in Canada.
I have placed that on the record, Mr. Speaker. I shall be able to refer to it without repeating it on other occasions. The choice is the choice of those on the other side as to which course we follow from this point on. I have dealt with one subject which I was prompted to do by the remarks that were made here tonight and earlier. I wish now to deal with the remark that was made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). Of course, Mr. Speaker, that vacant look of surprise on the minister's face is a perfectly natural expression to which we are all accustomed. Nevertheless, it is a perfectly natural expression for a man who returns after a long absence to surroundings which now must almost seem strange to him.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
From the Conservative
benches.

I was interested in one of the remarks made by the hon. member for Northumberland, Ont. with regard to the budget itself which he finds to be so satisfactory. He asked us where there could be any savings in this budget. Without attempting to cover too broad a field with regard to the many places where savings can be made- and many of them have been suggested- may I remind every hon. member that we have had dramatic evidence recently of how
The Budget-Mr. Drew money can be saved. That has been furnished by what happened at Petawawa.
Do you endorse Ross Thatcher?
Order.

The Petawawa incident is something which does more than merely raise the necessity for charges being laid. It is a great deal more than that. Let us remember that this is not the first time that there have been extensive thefts from camps here in Canada. This is not the first time that there have been warnings to the Department of National Defence that it was necessary that there be careful supervision of the military establishments of this country. There was, for instance-apart from other lootings in other camps-the dramatic episode at Farnham in Quebec where, for all practical purposes, it was discovered in December, 1949, that a whole camp had disappeared. That camp was equipped with plumbing, electrical fixtures, wiring, sinks, showers, refrigerators and all the things that go along with camps.
Was that Sam Hughes?

That camp disappeared except for a few of the walls and the foundations which could not be conveniently moved. Of more than 100 wooden structures-and very solid wooden structures they were-in that huge camp area, an undisclosed number had been lifted intact from their foundations by a heavy-tracked vehicle and sold for prices ranging from $25 to $50 to farmers and other residents in the eastern townships at that time.
That incident surely should have been a warning of the necessity for effective supervision of the valuable property under the control of the Department of National Defence. But other events have gone on which were or should have been a warning to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), and the responsibility must be his under our system of responsible government. Last June here in Ottawa there was a fire which did damage to the extent of $731,332.88, according to the returns tabled in this house. That was on June 2. On June 6 the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) met the Minister of Justice_
In his seat.

-spoke to him in his seat in
this house, and told him that he was able to furnish him with the names of men who could swear that paint, raincoats and other materials of that kind, and of the nature of those that had been in this building which was burned on June 2, had been offered for sale on the streets of the city of Ottawa. He

The Budget-Mr. Drew told the same thing to the Minister of National Defence on June 12.
June 13.

Or on June 13. It was indicated that those names were available. Naturally the hon. member for Peterborough West expected that he would be requested by the appropriate officials to give the names so that these could be followed up. Nothing was done. That was only one of a number of fires last year which resulted in damage which reached a total in value of $1,438,354.87. Nor have those fires stopped. For the first two months of this year there were fires that cost this country, according to the government's figures, $3,173,442.27. The thing that is very noticeable about these fires is the number of occasions on which they occurred in places where goods and equipment, and things that might be disposed of, have been stored. After all, what more effective way to make it impossible to check on the amount of the remaining stores of any kind could there possibly be than to have a fire which would destroy part of the stores and make it quite uncertain as to what had been there when the fire started?
Let us simply consider what happened at Petawawa. This extraordinary series of thefts was not discovered by anyone in the Department of National Defence. These carload thefts were not discovered by this department that had warnings for years of looting and thefts as well as of the danger of fire. It came to light only because of the integrity, because of the honesty and the sense of public duty, of the wife of one of the men in that camp. She, knowing that her husband was being approached by a participant in this nefarious scheme, reported it, as it was her duty to report it, and a duty which she fulfilled, to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. But it was not the Department of National Defence. So far as they are concerned, the chances are, so far as any record would suggest, that these thefts would still be going on if it had not been that someone was approached whose honesty itself was the safeguard of this country.
If it were not so serious in what it implies in a break-down of morale in certain sections of that organization-and certain very limited sections of that organization-this thing would be laughable. Who ever heard of any organized thefts which had reached the effrontery of stealing a whole railway siding?
Tracks and all.

Tracks and all. Theft is certainly becoming a fairly confirmed habit when the temptation to lift rails from a siding cannot be resisted by those who were carrying

out this operation on such a grand scale. And there appears no likelihood that this would have been discovered, although all this was under the supervision of the Department of National Defence. It so happened that these rails belonged to a railway company. The report suggests that they belonged to the Canadian Pacific Railway. Of course, so far we have only the reports, but reports written in a manner to suggest that they were from people who had made inquiries on the spot.
The officials were challenged in regard to the absence of this track. They indicated their surprise, and I have no doubt that the surprise interpreted itself in a proper admonition to those who had been so careless in their operation. But, according to reports- and these are the reports, after all, that the public received-not to be stymied by anything of that kind they went and tore up another track and replaced the rails in that way.
It is ludicrous, Mr. Speaker, but it is the sort of thing that indicates a complete breakdown of any measure of supervision by-
Better anchor it.
Yes, they should have anchored it, as one of the Liberal members suggested. They should have anchored that baby tank that got away.
They had better watch some of the branch lines of the C.N.R.
The fact is that in so far as we have yet been informed these carload thefts include stoves, electric refrigerators and things of that kind-
Everything that was loose.

-in substantial quantities. The fact is that anything that was loose went, and even things that were fairly tight went as well until they were discovered.
This wholesale looting is not just the responsibility of a few men whose names have been mentioned in the newspapers. This could not have happened if the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) had paid the slightest attention to the repeated warnings in this house that looting was taking place and that steps should be taken to safeguard government property in this country. These things would not have happened even, in all probability, if the Minister of National Defence had acted on the clear and positive information furnished him by the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) last June. These things would not have happened if a proper system of supervision had been established in any of the camps.

Most hon. members have had military service of some kind, and most of them know that almost to the point of annoyance the very first thing that is insisted upon in any military establishment is a daily accounting for the stores for which you are responsible; and officers and N.C.O.'s are detailed for the express purpose of checking over daily, or at regular intervals, things that are under government control.
This great camp at Petawawa, with an investment not by the government but by the people of Canada of many, many millions of dollars, was a place where any sort of efficient organization under the Department of National Defence would have prevented a thing of this kind happening before it even started. These series of thefts, the disappearing camp at Farnham, the fires in government stores amounting to millions of dollars, the thefts at Petawawa, and the other reports that have been presented to this house of the looting of government property, all have suggested for a long time the most detailed and exhaustive examination of the Department of National Defence.
The Minister of National Defence tells us there are inquiries. What kind of inquiries? I asked him today under what authority Mr. Currie had been appointed, and he has promised to inform me, but I must admit that it has not been possible yet to find under what order in council, or other order, Mr. Currie has been appointed.
It is not a few men at Petawawa, Mr. Speaker, who are on trial; it is not a few men with whom they were in contact who are on trial. It is the Department of National Defence that is on trial. It is the Department of National Defence that should be brought before a proper tribunal and made to account for its handling of government property, and that is particularly true at a time when this department is asking for a blank cheque of more than $2 billion of the people's money.
If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) wants to find places where he can save money, now that he has returned to the fold, may I suggest that he ask the government that an order in council be passed appointing an appropriate body which will have the full authority to inquire into every activity of the government, including the activities of the minister himself. I have heard the suggestion that this is something for the defence committee. Members of this house know just how freely the defence committee is being permitted to go into matters at this time. But, Mr. Speaker, I pointed out on an earlier occasion that the terms of reference of the committee on defence expenditures are not wide
The Budget-Mr. Drew enough to embrace the kind of inquiry which should be conducted into the inefficiency, gross negligence and failure properly to administer public property, which has already been disclosed by this series of events to which I * have referred.
When I speak of the minister being accountable, naturally I am speaking of his being accountable only in his capacity as a minister of the crown. In view of certain statements that I have seen reported in the press, even made by a Liberal member, asking that there be some scapegoat for the minister among the officials in the department for the incompetence and failure of that department in regard to the foot-and-mouth disease, I would point out that under our system the man responsible for the effective administration of his department is the minister. ^ And when a matter of this kind occurs, it is the minister who should explain, before some body that can take evidence in the proper manner, exactly what the circumstances were, what directions were given, what measure of control there was or what lack of control there was, in regard to these matters which are of' so much importance to us.
Now, these are matters which certainly are worthy of the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). But one thing more. The Minister of Finance made a statement in his budget speech of April 8 which carries us beyond this immediate point-and I leave that point with the recommendation, which I make in all earnestness, that the Minister of Finance, while this budget debate is still on, will urge the appointment of an appropriate body to conduct an inquiry into that department which is asking for approximately naif of the vast sum which he seeks to raise from the Canadian taxpayers this year.
But when we examine that huge sum, in the light of what he has said, we find that on April 8 he told us-and these are his words-
I expect there will be a shortfall of expenditures below the amounts provided by parliament in the appropriation votes.
Mr. Speaker, without some explanation, which has not yet been made, that statement means one thing, and one thing only. It means that the minister expects that he is actually going to tax the people beyond the amount he actually requires. That is something he has no right to do. It is something he has no right to ask us to support. From medieval days our system of parliament has rested upon the assumption that parliament could rely upon the figures presented by the minister of finance, and that it could rely upon the fact that, to the best of his knowledge, he was placing before the House of

The Budget-Mr. Drew Commons the figures which represented what he thought would be required from the people for the tasks the government expected to be called upon to undertake.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did that this year, too.
Then, if he did it this year, it would be interesting to know what he means when he tells us that he expects the expenditure will be less than the amount for which he is asking.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said by how much.
Oh-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, I did; read the speech again.

This speech is perfectly clear, and it clearly indicates the expectation that once again, to use the words of the minister, there is going to be a shortfall of expenditures below the amounts set out in the appropriation votes.
Already tonight the suggestion has been made that it was a commendable thing that surpluses be used to reduce debt. The repetition of that statement merely indicates how dangerous a state of mind some of the members of this house are actually in at this time. No member has raised any question about the wisdom of paying off debts at the appropriate time. But what has been questioned is the right of this government, or any other government under our parliamentary system, to raise funds for one purpose and to appropriate them for something else.
If it is intended to tax our people, to overtax our people, in the way the government is doing, then let the government say what the moneys are for. If they are for the payment of debt, then say so-and, upon reasonable explanation, doubtless the minister would receive support from the house. But the trouble is that the minister's record is so bad that members of this house have no reason to expect that anything that he puts before them will have any relation whatever to the facts as they will ultimately appear.
The last budget proved, by the most convincing demonstration that there could possibly be, the need for the most exacting review of every detail of the government's estimates before us, and for the most exacting review of the budget itself. After all, could anyone imagine a better piece of evidence of the slipshod and careless way in which last year's budget was prepared than what happened in the case of certain high incomes in this country?
Until such time as the Minister of Finance is prepared to say that he has reached the conclusion that there is some point at which


some people should receive not only nothing, but should receive less than nothing, then his budget of last year is simply evidence of slipshod methods in the preparation of the budget, no matter what his intentions might have been. Because he has disclosed quite clearly that at a certain level his taxes reached the point where they not only took the whole income, one hundred per cent of it, but in some cases taxed the people beyond their incomes.
Now, do not let him put on any smug appearance of glorying in taxing the rich. That was not his intention, as he disclosed. It was simply a result of slipshod methods, and now he seeks to rectify them. And nobody will know until next year whether he has or not, if he continues in the same way, and without any more willingness to review the facts than he displayed previously.
There is also this fact that should be borne in mind. There have been inquiries going on now for the last couple of days which have disclosed, as a result of the brilliant and untiring efforts of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), the utter breakdown of the supervision of the Department of Agriculture over an extremely important aspect of agricultural activity in this country.
What has been disclosed there, as is clearly set out in an article in Maclean's magazine, by Mr. Blair Fraser, is not merely negligence within a government department, but a failure to integrate the activities of that department in a manner which would have produced effective results.
There, again, is something with which the Minister of Finance should be dealing, not in this case in connection with the awful impact of the foot-and-mouth disease, but rather as to what it discloses in the way of a costly lack of integration of the efforts within that department.
These are only some of the things the Minister of Finance could be doing. Therefore I return to the request that has been made before, that if the committee on defence expenditures is, in fact, to be a committee which can carry out the terms of reference under which it operates, then it should not be confined to things that have happened m the past; but all the defence estimates for the coming year should forthwith be referred to that committee, as were the estimates of the Department of External Affairs.
I close these remarks with the request to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that, just as he moved that the estimates of the Department of External Affairs be referred to a committee, he likewise move that the estimates of the Department of National Defence be referred forthwith to the committee on

defence expenditures. May I suggest at the same time to the Prime Minister that he advise the chairman of that committee to act in a manner which will suggest reasons for confidence that the committee really intends to inquire into the affairs of the Department of National Defence.
We are dealing with a budget which means $343 on the average from every man, woman and child in Canada during the coming year, or a total of $1,715 on the average from every family of five in this country. These taxes can and should be reduced. I have suggested' ways in which the Minister of Finance, if he will make his recommendations to the government, can reduce expenditures and thus reduce the crushing burden of taxation during the coming year.

Mr. Speaker, what I have to say in the few moments I shall take to say it will have reference to that part of the speech of the hon. gentleman that had to do with family allowances. All I can say to him is that while I may not be a good enough scholar of Shakespeare to appreciate the quotation he gave the house I do know of another quotation from Shakespeare that might fit this particular occasion. My hon. friend will remember the words in Hamlet which Shakespeare immortalized: The lady doth protest too much, methinks.
Reference was made the other night to my hon. friend's earlier views on family allowances arising out of comments that were made by myself regarding a proposal to increase the present family allowance payments. I went on to say that since there was in one quarter of the house a desire that that should be done one could but conclude that there was now general agreement in this house with one exception-that exception of course being my amiable friend, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher)-as to the merits of the present Family Allowances Act.
I noted, as I think is historically the case, that the then acting leader of the opposition, the hon. member for Peel, had on July 25, 1944, moved an amendment to the Family Allowances Act which would have had the effect of giving the Family Allowances Act a period of suspension for many months. As one looks hurriedly at Hansard he cannot help but agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who said on that occasion, and I quote from page 5345 of Hansard, volume V, 1944:
I regret that the constitutional argument has been introduced at this time by the official opposition. I
The Budget-Mr. Martin
think that was a move to shelve this important matter, and I am glad, Mr. Speaker, that your ruling has been sustained.
That was the situation at that time. Undoubtedly the amendment brought in by the then leader of the opposition would have had the effect of shelving the present Family Allowances Act. I want my hon. friend to know that the reference that was made to his views on Monday night was not a paraphrasing by me, for I used words which he was reported in the press to have uttered. He did not take me to task; he did not say that those words were incorrectly reported; but he went on tonight to explain what his view was, not only in 1944 but in 1945, one year later, when it was apparent to everyone in the country, including the then premier of Ontario, that family allowances were indeed very popular and acceptable to the people of Canada.
I take it that my hon. friend is fully convinced now that the present Family Allowances Act is one that deserves the support of the people and if he should perchance ever become prime minister of this country he will never repeal the existing measure. I put that question to him three years ago and he made no comment. I take it that I interpret correctly what his position would be if that were to eventuate.
I do not wish to interrupt-

-the hon. minister-

No.

Sit down.
Then he went on-
I thought it was a question and I was going to answer.
I am sorry the hon. gentleman interrupts. He concluded his observations. He was entitled to make a defence, just as he is entitled now to protest against his discarded opinions.
Nonsense.

But I rather deprecate that he should have brought in the question of national unity. I did not raise that issue. I quoted from one source only; that was the hon. gentleman himself. He will find nothing in what I said the other night that is at all inconsistent with what I have tried to do all my life-
It had nothing to do with the issue before the house, nor has this.

In that speech the hon. gentleman went on:
Many millions of dollars from the pockets of the people of Ontario would go to the province of Quebec under this measure. But 1 assure you that the government of Ontario intends to do everything within its power to make sure that this iniquitous bill does not go into effect. It is not this bill alone-
These are the significant words.
It is not this bill alone but the whole principle involved-
Not this bill alone but the principle of family allowances.
No, no.

The hon. gentleman continued:
-but the whole principle involved which we intend to resist. If our money is to be used under the agreement then it is to be used for total war.
Lest there be any misunderstanding about the interpretation I place on what my hon. friend said, I am going to quote from an editorial in the Ottawa Journal of August 11, 1944; and I believe I have current justification for thinking the Journal would not misinterpret anything the hon. gentleman said. The heading was, "Premier Drew on Family Allowances" and the editorial went on:
When the government first introduced family allowances, the Journal said that apart from the measure's objeetional dole principle, plus its dangerous mortgaging of the future national income, the proposal held a threat to national unity. We based the last claim upon the disparity between our different provinces in the matter of large families, or, to be more specific, upon the preponderance of large families in the province of Quebec.
Those were not the words of my hon. friend. That is the first paragraph in the editorial. I do not know who wrote it, but recognizing the language I have my own idea. It goes on:
Now comes Premier Drew of Ontario to bring this issue into the open; to state it with a force and in a way to challenge grave reflections. Says he:
"When Ontario handed over certain of its taxing powers (to the federal government) the reason for doing so and the conditions under which the transfer was made were so that the government and parliament of Canada could wage total war."

The Budget-Mr. Martin
They are now quoting the leader of the opposition, as premier of Ontario.
"This family allowance bill is an obvious bribe . . . there is every reason why it should meet with approval in Quebec where there was a very important election approaching . . . Millions of dollars from the pockets of the people of Ontario will go to the province of Quebec under this measure . . . The people of Ontario will be asked to pay nearly half of the $200 million which will be needed as the initial amount to put the Family Allowances Act into effect.
Our attitude toward any measure which takes money from the pockets of the people of Ontario for the special advantage of Quebec is based upon considerations which affect that province alone. You know what those considerations are.
You know that we face an issue here in Canada hardly less important in its bearing upon our future than the outcome of the war itself. Temporizing will no longer do . . . We are paying the penalty of appeasement . . . Silence has been mistaken for weakness . . ."
No one need be in doubt about Mr. Drew's meaning. He may be right or wrong; he at least is honest and clear. Little sense exists in efforts to gloss over the fact that, in the main, he is right . . .
Nor need any doubt exist that in the matter of gain from this family allowance measure Quebec's share will be out of all proportion to that of Ontario . . .
I am not going to speak at length; I am just going to refer to some other editorials. On September 30, 1944, again in the Ottawa Journal, will be found an article dealing with the hon. gentleman's views on family allowances. There was another on February 23, 1945, in which I find this:
Premier Drew's August 9 radio address, in which he declared that the "iniquitous bill" (the Family Allowances Act) would be resisted by Ontario, was quoted in part by Mr. Hepburn. Reading from a copy of the radio address, Mr. Hepburn quoted the paragraph in which the premier spoke of Ontario's money going to the province of Quebec under the Family Allowances Act.
"It is one thing to say, as the premier says-
And this is the point I made a while ago.
that the province should have been consulted," said Mr. Jolliffe, "and it is an entirely different thing to say that this measure will be resisted by every means within the power of the government. I assume Ontario families will receive payment under the act in July, and I do not suppose the government will attempt to intercept the allowances."

Was that Mr. Jolliffe or
Mr. Hepburn? You mentioned both names.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Hepburn first and Mr. Jolliffe second. The hon. gentleman will recognize those two gentlemen as distinguished contemporaries in another legislative field.
I recognize them as authorities you would follow.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
They are not authorities, but they are witnesses as to what my hon. friend's views were at that time. The fact is that these quotations, some of which I have given in extenso and some of which I have

The Budget-Mr. Martin paraphrased, and others in which I have given dates and references, can be looked up by any hon. member. I say to the hon gentleman, as I said the other night, that as the minister responsible for the administration of this measure I welcome the fact that, in spite of the reservation he has made tonight, at least he now accepts the important principle of family allowances. But since he has raised the issue-
Just the same as ever.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: My hon. friend groans. 1 suppose if I were in a similar situation I would groan too.
You cannot follow a straight line for thirty seconds.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
In his speech tonight the hon. gentleman challenged me to support what I had said in this house last Monday evening. I leave it to this house and to the hon. gentleman if I have not been accurate and fair. I sincerely hope I have convinced the hon. gentleman that we should not disturb the present Family Allowances Act.
On motion of Mr. Abbott the debate was adjourned.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
